key_facts: **Trichotillomania** is recurrent hair pulling causing hair loss: a **body-focused repetitive behaviour** (OCD-related disorder).
Irregular patches with hairs of **different lengths**, broken hairs, often on the side of the dominant hand; scalp, brows, lashes.
Many deny pulling; dermoscopy shows broken hairs, coiled hairs and 'flame' hairs.
First-line: **habit reversal therapy** (CBT); treat associated anxiety or depression.
Ask about **trichophagia** (eating hair): risk of trichobezoar.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Trichotillomania** (hair-pulling disorder) is a body-focused repetitive behaviour causing noticeable hair loss. It is not scarring in early disease. It is commoner in children and adolescents and often under-disclosed.

sub: 1–2% lifetime; children (often self-limiting) and young women; associated with anxiety, OCD and depression.

ul: Classed with obsessive–compulsive related disorders; anxiety, boredom or sensory urge often precede pulling.
**Automatic** pulling (unaware, while reading/screens) vs **focused** pulling (conscious tension relief).
May coexist with skin picking or nail biting.
**"It's just a bad habit"**: it is a recognised mental health condition that responds to specific therapy.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Repeated pulling **mechanically breaks** hairs, which regrow normally if pulling stops.

mech.t: Tension or boredom builds; pulling gives relief or pleasure, reinforcing the behaviour.
Hairs fracture at different lengths; follicles bleed or become distorted.
Follicles are not destroyed early on, so hair regrows if pulling stops; chronic pulling can scar.

histo: Rarely needed: trichomalacia, pigment casts, empty follicles and increased catagen hairs without inflammation.

ul: Irregular, angular or tonsure-like patches; hairs of **unequal lengths**; broken hairs firmly anchored.
Common sites: vertex, frontotemporal (dominant-hand side), brows and lashes.
Trichoscopy: black dots, broken hairs, **V-sign**, flame hairs — contrast with AA exclamation marks.
Chronic severe pulling can eventually scar; secondary infection/crust possible.

sub: Early-onset pulling often settles; support parents without punishment.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical pattern ± behaviour history (ask privately, without blame). Pull test negative. Exclude tinea if scaly. Differentiate from [alopecia areata](condition:alopecia-areata) and [scarring alopecia](condition:scarring-alopecia).

ddx.name: Alopecia areata
ddx.f: Smooth patch; exclamation hairs; positive edge pull test

ul: Validate and reduce shame; involve parents/carers sensitively in children.
**Habit-reversal training / CBT** via CAMHS, psychology or specialist services is first-line.
Stimulus control (fidget tools, gloves at night, shorter nails); treat secondary infection if present.
Medicines are not first-line in primary care; any drug therapy is specialist.

refer.t: Abdominal pain, early satiety, vomiting, weight loss, halitosis, epigastric mass → urgent surgical review (trichobezoar / Rapunzel syndrome).
Self-harm or suicidal ideation → urgent mental-health assessment.
Diagnostic doubt or progressive scarring → dermatology.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Abdominal pain, early satiety, vomiting, weight loss, halitosis, epigastric mass → urgent surgical review (trichobezoar / Rapunzel syndrome).
Self-harm or suicidal ideation → urgent mental-health assessment.
Diagnostic doubt or progressive scarring → dermatology.
Permanent alopecia, infection, shame and social isolation; trichobezoar.
Chronic and fluctuating in adults; good outcomes with habit reversal therapy.

pearls: Different hair lengths in one patch is the bedside clue.
Eyebrow/eyelash pulling in a child is still trichotillomania until proven otherwise — also consider AA and hypothyroidism for lateral brows.
Steroids will not fix the behaviour.

quiz.q: When should you think of Trichotillomania?
quiz.a: Irregular or geometric bald patch with hairs of many different lengths; pull test negative; often on the dominant-hand side.
Body-focused repetitive behaviour (OCRD spectrum) — automatic or focused pulling; broken shafts, not autoimmune bulb attack.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Non-judgemental recognition, habit-reversal / CBT referral, wound care if excoriated; do not treat as alopecia areata with steroids alone.
Trichophagia with abdominal pain, vomiting or mass → urgent surgical assessment for trichobezoar.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Abdominal pain, early satiety, vomiting, weight loss, halitosis, epigastric mass → urgent surgical review (trichobezoar / Rapunzel syndrome).
